title: B.C. urged to probe deaths of natives in police custody
article: Native leaders in British Columbia want the provincial government to investigate why so many aboriginal people have died after being arrested by police.
"You know, it doesn't make sense," Harley Desjarlais, president of the Métis Council of British Columbia, said in an interview yesterday as he contemplated the numbers.
Six aboriginal men have died in as many years after being arrested by police in Prince George, Williams Lake, Vancouver and Oak Bay.
Clayton Willey, 33, of Prince George, died in July after police used a taser to knock him down so they could put him in an ambulance.
Darrell Paquette, 43, died last September after being subdued by police while being arrested in Prince George.
Paul Alphonse, 67, of Williams Lake, died in 2000 a week after he fought with police during his arrest.
Peter Prince, 64, died in 2001 in a Prince George prison cell.
Anthany Dawson, 29, had a cardiac arrest in 1999 after five police officers tackled him in Oak Bay, just outside Victoria, punching him repeatedly before loading him in an ambulance.
Frank Paul, 47, died in 1998 after Vancouver police dragged him out of the drunk tank on a cold December night and left him in a back alley where he froze.

Most of those deaths have already been investigated by the B.C. coroner's office, and through internal police reviews, with no fault to any police officers found. In the two most recent deaths, Mr. Willey's and Mr. Paquette's, inquests are pending and in a third, Mr. Paul's, a B.C. police complaints commission inquiry has been reactivated.

But in a letter that is being drafted this week, the province's top native leaders will ask the government to do more to find out what is behind the deaths -- and to take action to stop more from occurring.
Noting that three deaths have taken place in Prince George alone, in the past two years, Mr. Desjarlais said that is too many to be a coincidence.
"That's a fairly significant number regardless of whether they were aboriginal people or not. Three people dying in police custody would be a cause for concern -- but three natives?

"It's happening in other parts of the province. It's not just something that's exclusive to Prince George or anything like that, but it seems to be that if you are being brought into custody or are being apprehended your chances of actually dying during this encounter are a lot more substantial if you are aboriginal.
"Why is this the case?" Mr. Desjarlais asked.
"I think we would be remiss as leaders to dismiss it or accept claims that there were exceptional circumstances in all of these cases. Collectively they constitute a trend."

Stuart Phillip, president of the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, said the matter has been of concern to native leaders for several years, but it has come to a head because of the shocking nature of Mr. Paul's death and lingering questions about the deaths of the others.

"This is not a new issue. This is an ongoing and growing concern with the aboriginal people across the country. It doesn't appear to be isolated incidents. There appears to be a pattern here. There appears to be a double standard that aboriginal people are treated more harshly when they are taken into custody, than non-native people."
Mr. Phillip said native leaders want a meeting with the government "to open up a dialogue to see what measures can be undertaken to bring about a stop to this."

There is currently an inquiry under way in Saskatchewan into the 1990 death of Neil Stonechild, who was taken into custody by police, then dropped off outside Saskatoon, where he froze to death. And there continue to be calls for a public inquiry into the death of Dudley George, who was shot by police at Ipperwash, Ont., in 1995.
